Sinking in Potholes

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Potholes, potholes, everywhere - and so are Carte Blanche viewers, exposing the hazardous state of South Africa's decaying road network.

Unique Selling Point:
This year's season of heat waves and rain, a stormy cocktail perfect for cracking up South Africa's roads, has exposed the country's state of disrepair. A nationwide plague of potholes has become the physical representation of the accelerating decay of South Africa’s infrastructure.
After our social media call for viewer submissions we have almost four hundred photos and videos from all over the country. Potholes are everywhere and what better way to illustrate this than the viewers’ submissions.
We start the story with light-hearted moments - from the pothole fishing competition in KZN to the man bathing waste deep in a pothole. But, Potholes are a serious matter...

Summary:
Dr Louis Roodt, pothole specialist engineer, examines some viewer contributions, with an emphasis on road safety, and explains grade/severity of potholes, how they should be maintained and the consequences of leaving it too late. He also expands on the crumbling infrastructure, where roads are not being given the priority that people projects are. Dr Louis Roodt is based in Hermanus, so may need to send Michael Duffet to shoot.
Case study August Morena travels the notorious R555 to Middleburg on which he has witnessed fatal accidents. August drives on the R555 once a week and has lost many tyres over the years at huge cost. It is well known in the area as a very dangerous road – a main problem being rain, if it rains the R555 becomes extremely dangerous because drivers cannot see the potholes. The road has been in a state of disrepair for years. We have planned to go on a road trip on the R555 with August.
Another case study is a location, the JRA Asphalt factory in Johannesburg. R 63 million was spent on refurbishing the existing plant – it has not produced anything since March 2020, has never met production targets and is still an empty yard – even though the JRA has put out ads for plant supervisors.
Additionally in Johannesburg, JRA depots are under-resourced – people doing nothing. We can go on site visits with Sean Kreusch (DA).
There are other examples to pepper the story with, and also, how does the pothole situation relate to the economy, who is to blame and what can be done about it?

Further information:
Transport Economist Prof John Maluleke speaks on the Integrated Transport Plan (ITP) handed down to municipal level from government budget – pinpointing that there are not enough skilled people to implement it properly. The allocations are adequate if used correctly using expert suppliers – but procurement, supply chain management and training issues need to be rectified – Maluleke says he would supply training for free, that’s how passionate he is.
Economist Dawie Roodt focuses on the big picture - fiscus and government that for political reasons have made a priority of spending more money on grants, housing, etc. Such that, there is not enough money left to invest in infrastructure which is what keeps an economy ticking over, and viable.
Mutchutshu Nxumalo as former President of SARF has a complete overview of the potholes/roads crisis.
Minister of Transport Fikile Mbalula will be given opportunity to reply. What is being done to address the poor state of our roads? Is there enough budget to fix what appears to be breaking down everywhere in the country. In his tweet to a person who brought to his attention a fatality caused by a pothole, Mbalula laid the responsibility on municipalities, or rather, provincial level. But what accountability is there, on the side of government at a national level, to ensure that provinces maintain and upkeep their roads to the right safety standards?
Two case studies concerning practical solutions are:
1. KOGA District, Eastern Cape example – cheaper roads constructed using plastic at half the price of conventional methods. Engineer Gareth Nel, involved in the project, can speak to this (in Cape Town), but we are able rather to get footage from him.
2. Pro-Phalt – proposing public private partnership with investment from big business in exchange for brand exposure to employ their patented infra-red machine to repair potholes more cleanly and efficiently. [ not confirmed, they are still busy with the initiative – it may be too much ]
Further examples of pothole incidents:
1. Incident of a Ford Fortuna swallowed up by a sink hole.
2. North Riding – Lack of expertise/supervision, speaks to the question, are the right contractors being used. Road was freshly tarred about 2 months ago. Problem is, they covered manholes and storm water drains in the process and the new white road markings are already fading.
3. KZN – Taxi drivers and farmers protesting together about the terrible state of their roads – possibly only use visuals of this.
Have already Joburg potholes footage shot by Philasande
Links at Houghton Golf Club pothole – and various other potholes.

Press Release:


Dodging potholes has become a matter of life and death on many South African roads. Has a nationwide plague of potholes become the symbol for the accelerating decay and neglect of the country’s infrastructure?

Script:


VO: This is the R triple 5, en route to Limpopo. For many years electronic engineer August Morena has been commuting monthly from Johannesburg to his home in Burgersfort. He believes he's lucky to be alive, because a 96 kilometer stretch of this road is so treacherous.

August: From Middelburg side to Mapochs mine, there's potholes all over the place, I've suffered a lot on that road. Myself and my wife had to sleep at the side of the road because I lost two tires on my vehicle.

LINK: A pothole is not just a hole in the road. In the context of South Africa, it has become a symbol of a decaying road network, and an infrastructure that is crumbling right before our eyes, or underneath the wheels of our cars.

Louis: A pothole is the physical manifestation of a systematic breakdown in preventative maintenance.

VO: And by studying potholes, Dr Louis Roodt a civil engineer, warns that these gaping wounds on our roads must be attended to.

Louis: [00:00:46.13] When it comes to safety, the reasonable driver can expect a road that is reasonably safe for its intended use. That is a legal principle.

VO: As A signatory to the 2011 UN Safety Declaration, South Africa committed to halving road fatalities by 2020. This target was never met, points out Mutshutshu Nxumalo, past president of the South African Road Federation.

Mutshutshu: The government was supposed to work towards safer roads because in our country, we travel a lot using roads because we don't have a good public infrastructure.
Mac : How quickly should a pothole be fixed?
Mutshutshu: Once a pothole is reported, it should be attended to within three days. And that's our standard in the country. But internationally, it should be attended within 24 hours because anything can go wrong because of that pothole.

VO: As is August Morena's experience of the R triple 5. Over the years he's seen the road claim many victims.

August: In February, I went home. It was a Sunday, there was a huge pothole whereby one of the vehicles was trying to avoid a pothole, and then it went into a head on collision with the oncoming traffic. Two weeks later, one vehicle went at the back of the bakkie, trying to avoid the same pothole, so it's dangerous.

VO: Littered along the tarmac the danger is glaring. When Carte Blanche called for viewers to submit their pothole horrors, our web and social pages were swamped, as recent heavy rains exposed the shocking state of the country's roads. Some light-hearted protests veiled a desperate plea for something to be done.
Louis: Curry's Post road, they're probably catching mudfish, that's the way South Africa deals with it, we can only laugh
VO: We asked Dr Roodt to pick out a few viewer posts to illustrate the magnitude of the problem.

Louis: This road has the symptoms of neglect over a long period of time. You can see scattered potholes there. All of them, very dangerous.
Once you've allowed the potholes to start developing, the pace of deterioration increases because the seal is open and water is the number one enemy of roads.// Second is traffic to then impact on that weakened road structure and make it fall apart.

LINK: So it's potholes like these that are very, very dangerous, especially near an intersection. In just the past 10 minutes that we've been here, cars have tried to avoid it, almost hit our cameraman, and can even cause accidents because of gaping holes like this on our roads.

Mutshutshu: The current figures R142 billion lost to the economy due to accidents or incidents on the roads

VO: And potholes are responsible for between 5 and 10% of those incidents.

Louis: The cost of fixing a pothole would be in the order of less than R1000. But if that pothole results in an accident where a vehicle overturns, and people are killed or rendered quadriplegics, the claim could be R10 million.

Mutshutshu: The roads are an asset for everyone.It's not an asset for one person who is poor or rich. We come from home to work, go to schools, go to hospitals. It will not be less than R5 trillion to replace the road infrastructure that we have.

VO: The 10th largest road network in the world is taking strain, as the shrinking national budget is prioritising social needs and debt repayment, while roads take a back seat.

Mutshutshu: We have been having about 4% allocation to roads, which includes even new infrastructure. We were supposed to have 10% to maintain our infrastructure properly.

VO: This shortfall is now critical. Typically the lifespan of a road is about eight to ten years, but it has to be maintained to prevent having to rebuild, before the end of its design life of 25 years.
Louis: It is not the rain that is the underlying cause of the problem. What is now suddenly a national explosion in potholes could have been prevented with proper seals and drainage management.
VO: which is why paved roads in six out of nine provinces are in dire condition, with the Free State being the worst, prompting demonstrations from Farmers and Taxi Drivers in Ficksburg.
Louis: The current network in South Africa especially at provincial level, has deteriorated over years

VO: With around 750 000 kilometers of road network, proclaimed paved roads form about 163 000, so there is pressure on government to upgrade the backlog of around 455 000 kilometers of gravel road. Deputy Minister of Transport Dikeledi Magadzi, admits that particularly municipal roads are in bad shape.

Dikeledi: Money will never be sufficient to be able to deal with infrastructure because you maintain at the same time you must develop. The maintenance grant that the national department is always giving to the provinces and municipalities is never sufficient.

VO: It's towns like Standerton Mpumalanga that lie forgotten,// steeped in decay,// as traffic dances and bounces in ordered disarray around its scarred and mottled tar//- and not without some near misses.//
Mutshutshu: Here we have potholes that have been reported maybe for years and not attended to.
Mac: Where's the disconnect? No matter how many complaints you log, nothing ever happens.
Mutshutshu: The authority that is in charge, whether it's a municipal road, If it goes to the provincial department, If it's a road agency, they must take responsibility.
VO: //But Standerton is not alone, there are many neglected towns that mirror a similar state of infrastructure decline.

Louis: We often see Kimberley in the news for the wrong reasons and one of them being that sewage runs all over the road. Belfast, there's just a complete lack of doing the basics, which in terms of our extended Public Works programme can be funded from national government.

VO: Off route from the highly regarded SANRAL national roads, the economic hub of Gauteng has not come off unscathed, with road surfaces visibly disintegrating. To compound matters, a 63 million rands refurbishment of an old asphalt plant in Johannesburg, that would potentially solve some of the city's road infrastructure challenges, lay dormant for months.

Sean: It was scheduled to produce anything between 110 to 150 thousand tons per annum. Unfortunately, the best we could see in the last report was that it produced its own 18,000 tonnes within a year.

VO: DA Shadow MMC for transport Johannesburg, Sean Kreusch is one amongst many campaigning for effective service delivery on roads.

Sean: We are in a crisis and patching potholes is merely alleviating the pain for now but the pain will only go away when the JRA goes back to its mandate of proper road maintenance and an asphalt plant that delivers on its mandate

VO: The JRA finally put the asphalt plant back to work on the 1st of April, and is now on another Potholes repair blitz after fixing over 95000 potholes around the turn of the year.

LINK: So fixing a pothole isn't just about filling a hole. It Requires a whole set of procedures and people with the correct skills to do the job properly.

VO: Otherwise the problems recur and good money is thrown after bad.

Mutshutshu: The cost of the challenges we are faced with starts with the political deployments. In south africa, we have never had any minister that is technical in an infrastructure area. It's a disaster. The municipalities are also battling because of the same challenge.

Dikeledi: There is a programme that is funded by SANRAL and another programme that is funded by the Department, wherein we're working with several University, to make sure that we develop engineers. They will be deployed to municipalities and provinces.

VO: Solutions are what's needed, and some municipalities, like Kouga in the Eastern Cape, turned to alternative methods and built a three kilometre stretch of road, using a treated plastic road building technique that's cheaper.
And when it comes to patching - // this high tech infrared option can fix potholes within 20 minutes.//
VO: Even so, it's the tried and tested methods with a proven track record that should be applied right away, especially to high risk roads like the R triple 5.

August: We just say we are lucky if you arrive at your destination without hitting a single pothole. And we're just hoping that it doesn't rain because when it's raining it is more dangerous.

Dikeledi: It is now receiving attention as we're speaking. Not only are we talking about the roads in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, most of the roads are receiving attention.

Mutshutshu: The economy is on its knees, we are on our tummies.. And infrastructure is one of those elements that can actually ignite the economy to start running and be positive. If you put money on a road, you have brought in development.

VO: Instead of waiting around, for the country's ailing road network to be resuscitated, proactive citizens have taken to pothole patching. And at least there are some perks to a fractured infrastructure… when there's a shortage of water, simply visit your nearest pothole.

Over the years he's seen the road claim many victims. August: In February, I went home. It was a Sunday, there was a huge pothole whereby one of the vehicles was trying to avoid a pothole, and then it went into a head on collision with the oncoming traffic. Two weeks later, one vehicle went at the back of the bakkie, trying to avoid the same pothole, so it's dangerous. VO: Littered along the tarmac the danger is glaring. When Carte Blanche called for viewers to submit their pothole horrors, our web and social pages were swamped, as recent heavy rains exposed the shocking state of the country's roads. Some light-hearted protests veiled a desperate plea for something to be done. Louis: Curry's Post road, they're probably catching mudfish, that's the way South Africa deals with it, we can only laugh VO: We asked Dr Roodt to pick out a few viewer posts to illustrate the magnitude of the problem. Louis: This road has the symptoms of neglect over a long period of time. You can see scattered potholes there. All of them, very dangerous. Once you've allowed the potholes to start developing, the pace of deterioration increases because the seal is open and water is the number one enemy of roads.// Second is traffic to then impact on that weakened road structure and make it fall apart. LINK: So it's potholes like these that are very, very dangerous, especially near an intersection. In just the past 10 minutes that we've been here, cars have tried to avoid it, almost hit our cameraman, and can even cause accidents because of gaping holes like this on our roads. Mutshutshu: The current figures R142 billion lost to the economy due to accidents or incidents on the roads VO: And potholes are responsible for between 5 and 10% of those incidents. Louis: The cost of fixing a pothole would be in the order of less than R1000. But if that pothole results in an accident where a vehicle overturns, and people are killed or rendered quadriplegics, the claim could be R10 million. Mutshutshu: The roads are an asset for everyone.It's not an asset for one person who is poor or rich. We come from home to work, go to schools, go to hospitals. It will not be less than R5 trillion to replace the road infrastructure that we have. VO: The 10th largest road network in the world is taking strain, as the shrinking national budget is prioritising social needs and debt repayment, while roads take a back seat. Mutshutshu: We have been having about 4% allocation to roads, which includes even new infrastructure. We were supposed to have 10% to maintain our infrastructure properly. VO: This shortfall is now critical. Typically the lifespan of a road is about eight to ten years, but it has to be maintained to prevent having to rebuild, before the end of its design life of 25 years. Louis: It is not the rain that is the underlying cause of the problem. What is now suddenly a national explosion in potholes could have been prevented with proper seals and drainage management. VO: which is why paved roads in six out of nine provinces are in dire condition, with the Free State being the worst, prompting demonstrations from Farmers and Taxi Drivers in Ficksburg. Louis: The current network in South Africa especially at provincial level, has deteriorated over years VO: With around 750 000 kilometers of road network, proclaimed paved roads form about 163 000, so there is pressure on government to upgrade the backlog of around 455 000 kilometers of gravel road. Deputy Minister of Transport Dikeledi Magadzi, admits that particularly municipal roads are in bad shape. Dikeledi: Money will never be sufficient to be able to deal with infrastructure because you maintain at the same time you must develop. The maintenance grant that the national department is always giving to the provinces and municipalities is never sufficient. VO: It's towns like Standerton Mpumalanga that lie forgotten,// steeped in decay,// as traffic dances and bounces in ordered disarray around its scarred and mottled tar//- and not without some near misses.// Mutshutshu: Here we have potholes that have been reported maybe for years and not attended to. Mac: Where's the disconnect? No matter how many complaints you log, nothing ever happens. Mutshutshu: The authority that is in charge, whether it's a municipal road, If it goes to the provincial department, If it's a road agency, they must take responsibility. VO: //But Standerton is not alone, there are many neglected towns that mirror a similar state of infrastructure decline. Louis: We often see Kimberley in the news for the wrong reasons and one of them being that sewage runs all over the road. Belfast, there's just a complete lack of doing the basics, which in terms of our extended Public Works programme can be funded from national government. VO: Off route from the highly regarded SANRAL national roads, the economic hub of Gauteng has not come off unscathed, with road surfaces visibly disintegrating. To compound matters, a 63 million rands refurbishment of an old asphalt plant in Johannesburg, that would potentially solve some of the city's road infrastructure challenges, lay dormant for months. Sean: It was scheduled to produce anything between 110 to 150 thousand tons per annum. Unfortunately, the best we could see in the last report was that it produced its own 18,000 tonnes within a year. VO: DA Shadow MMC for transport Johannesburg, Sean Kreusch is one amongst many campaigning for effective service delivery on roads. Sean: We are in a crisis and patching potholes is merely alleviating the pain for now but the pain will only go away when the JRA goes back to its mandate of proper road maintenance and an asphalt plant that delivers on its mandate VO: The JRA finally put the asphalt plant back to work on the 1st of April, and is now on another Potholes repair blitz after fixing over 95000 potholes around the turn of the year. LINK: So fixing a pothole isn't just about filling a hole. It Requires a whole set of procedures and people with the correct skills to do the job properly. VO: Otherwise the problems recur and good money is thrown after bad. Mutshutshu: The cost of the challenges we are faced with starts with the political deployments. In south africa, we have never had any minister that is technical in an infrastructure area. It's a disaster. The municipalities are also battling because of the same challenge. Dikeledi: There is a programme that is funded by SANRAL and another programme that is funded by the Department, wherein we're working with several University, to make sure that we develop engineers. They will be deployed to municipalities and provinces. VO: Solutions are what's needed, and some municipalities, like Kouga in the Eastern Cape, turned to alternative methods and built a three kilometre stretch of road, using a treated plastic road building technique that's cheaper. And when it comes to patching - // this high tech infrared option can fix potholes within 20 minutes.// VO: Even so, it's the tried and tested methods with a proven track record that should be applied right away, especially to high risk roads like the R triple 5. August: We just say we are lucky if you arrive at your destination without hitting a single pothole. And we're just hoping that it doesn't rain because when it's raining it is more dangerous. Dikeledi: It is now receiving attention as we're speaking. Not only are we talking about the roads in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, most of the roads are receiving attention. Mutshutshu: The economy is on its knees, we are on our tummies.. And infrastructure is one of those elements that can actually ignite the economy to start running and be positive. If you put money on a road, you have brought in development. VO: Instead of waiting around, for the country's ailing road network to be resuscitated, proactive citizens have taken to pothole patching. And at least there are some perks to a fractured infrastructure… when there's a shortage of water, simply visit your nearest pothole.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Potholes, potholes, everywhere - and so are Carte Blanche viewers, exposing the hazardous state of South Africa's decaying road network.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This year's season of heat waves and rain, a stormy cocktail perfect for cracking up South Africa's roads, has exposed the country's state of disrepair. A nationwide plague of potholes has become the physical representation of the accelerating decay of South Africa’s infrastructure. After our social media call for viewer submissions we have almost four hundred photos and videos from all over the country. Potholes are everywhere and what better way to illustrate this than the viewers’ submissions. We start the story with light-hearted moments - from the pothole fishing competition in KZN to the man bathing waste deep in a pothole. But, Potholes are a serious matter...
metadata.Summary: Dr Louis Roodt, pothole specialist engineer, examines some viewer contributions, with an emphasis on road safety, and explains grade/severity of potholes, how they should be maintained and the consequences of leaving it too late. He also expands on the crumbling infrastructure, where roads are not being given the priority that people projects are. Dr Louis Roodt is based in Hermanus, so may need to send Michael Duffet to shoot. Case study August Morena travels the notorious R555 to Middleburg on which he has witnessed fatal accidents. August drives on the R555 once a week and has lost many tyres over the years at huge cost. It is well known in the area as a very dangerous road – a main problem being rain, if it rains the R555 becomes extremely dangerous because drivers cannot see the potholes. The road has been in a state of disrepair for years. We have planned to go on a road trip on the R555 with August. Another case study is a location, the JRA Asphalt factory in Johannesburg. R 63 million was spent on refurbishing the existing plant – it has not produced anything since March 2020, has never met production targets and is still an empty yard – even though the JRA has put out ads for plant supervisors. Additionally in Johannesburg, JRA depots are under-resourced – people doing nothing. We can go on site visits with Sean Kreusch (DA). There are other examples to pepper the story with, and also, how does the pothole situation relate to the economy, who is to blame and what can be done about it?
metadata.Further information: Transport Economist Prof John Maluleke speaks on the Integrated Transport Plan (ITP) handed down to municipal level from government budget – pinpointing that there are not enough skilled people to implement it properly. The allocations are adequate if used correctly using expert suppliers – but procurement, supply chain management and training issues need to be rectified – Maluleke says he would supply training for free, that’s how passionate he is. Economist Dawie Roodt focuses on the big picture - fiscus and government that for political reasons have made a priority of spending more money on grants, housing, etc. Such that, there is not enough money left to invest in infrastructure which is what keeps an economy ticking over, and viable. Mutchutshu Nxumalo as former President of SARF has a complete overview of the potholes/roads crisis. Minister of Transport Fikile Mbalula will be given opportunity to reply. What is being done to address the poor state of our roads? Is there enough budget to fix what appears to be breaking down everywhere in the country. In his tweet to a person who brought to his attention a fatality caused by a pothole, Mbalula laid the responsibility on municipalities, or rather, provincial level. But what accountability is there, on the side of government at a national level, to ensure that provinces maintain and upkeep their roads to the right safety standards? Two case studies concerning practical solutions are: 1. KOGA District, Eastern Cape example – cheaper roads constructed using plastic at half the price of conventional methods. Engineer Gareth Nel, involved in the project, can speak to this (in Cape Town), but we are able rather to get footage from him. 2. Pro-Phalt – proposing public private partnership with investment from big business in exchange for brand exposure to employ their patented infra-red machine to repair potholes more cleanly and efficiently. [ not confirmed, they are still busy with the initiative – it may be too much ] Further examples of pothole incidents: 1. Incident of a Ford Fortuna swallowed up by a sink hole. 2. North Riding – Lack of expertise/supervision, speaks to the question, are the right contractors being used. Road was freshly tarred about 2 months ago. Problem is, they covered manholes and storm water drains in the process and the new white road markings are already fading. 3. KZN – Taxi drivers and farmers protesting together about the terrible state of their roads – possibly only use visuals of this. Have already Joburg potholes footage shot by Philasande Links at Houghton Golf Club pothole – and various other potholes.
